CHAPTER 11: HUMAN RIGHTS PRINCIPLES

LEARNING OUTCOMES (5.1 AND 5.2)
- Explain what it means for human rights to be universal, inalienable and indivisible.
- Tell the difference between civil and political rights and economic, social and cultural rights.
- Explain absolute, limited and qualified rights.
- Explain negative rights and positive rights.
- Identify your rights to education in Bunreacht na hEireann (Article 42) and in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC, Articles 28 and 29).
- Identify the link between the UNCRC and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR).
- Explain 'rights holder' and 'duty bearer'.
- Use 'immediate obligation' and 'progressive realisation' to explain what it means for states to implement rights 'to the maximum extent of their available resources'.

INTRODUCTION: WHERE HUMAN RIGHTS CAME FROM
- Human rights act as a pillar of society, standing for equality and justice for all citizens.
- Ideas of justice and fairness go back to ancient times.
- The modern human rights movement took shape after World War II and the horrors of the Holocaust.
- The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the United Nations in 1948. It laid the foundations for today's human rights standards.
- The UDHR was a catalyst (a trigger) for international legal frameworks to enforce human rights and hold countries accountable.
- The UN and its agencies monitor human rights in different countries and investigate when violations happen.
- Civil society, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and grassroots movements also protect human rights by raising awareness and campaigning.
- A video in the chapter notes that if you asked 20 different people what human rights are, you would get 20 different answers.

11.1 HUMAN RIGHTS BASICS - KEY TERMS
- Human rights: the rights we have simply because we are human.
- Universal: all people everywhere in the world are entitled to human rights. Article 1 of the UDHR: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'
- Inalienable: human rights should not be taken away, except in a specific situation. Example: your right to move freely was limited during the Covid-19 restrictions.
- Indivisible: all human rights are indivisible and interdependent. One set of rights cannot be enjoyed without the others. All rights have equal status, and denying one right blocks enjoyment of others.
- Economic, social and cultural rights: include the right to adequate housing, education, food, to take part in cultural life, and to work.
- Civil and political rights: protect your individual freedoms and your right to take part in the civil and political life of your state without discrimination. Example: the right to take part in your government.

THE 30 ARTICLES OF THE UDHR (SIMPLE VERSION)
- 1 Equality: everyone is born free and equal in dignity and rights.
- 2 Freedom from discrimination.
- 3 Life, liberty and personal security.
- 4 Freedom from slavery or servitude.
- 5 Freedom from torture and cruel or degrading treatment.
- 6 Recognition as a person before the law.
- 7 Equality before the law.
- 8 Remedy by a competent tribunal.
- 9 Freedom from arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.
- 10 Right to a fair public hearing.
- 11 Innocent until proven guilty.
- 12 Privacy: no-one may interfere with your privacy, family or home.
- 13 Freedom of movement in and out of the country.
- 14 Right to seek asylum in other countries from persecution.
- 15 Right to a nationality.
- 16 Right to marriage and to raise a family.
- 17 Right to own property.
- 18 Freedom of belief and religion.
- 19 Freedom of opinion and expression.
- 20 Freedom of peaceful assembly and association.
- 21 Right to take part in the government of your country.
- 22 Right to social security.
- 23 Right to desirable work and to join trade unions.
- 24 Right to rest and leisure.
- 25 Right to an adequate standard of living: food, clothing, housing and medical care.
- 26 Right to education.
- 27 Right to participate in the cultural life of the community.
- 28 Right to a social order that articulates this document.
- 29 Mutual responsibility: we all have a responsibility to protect the rights and freedoms of the people around us.
- 30 Freedom from state or personal interference: nothing in the declaration justifies any person or country taking away these rights.

ABSOLUTE, LIMITED AND QUALIFIED RIGHTS
- Absolute rights: cannot lawfully be interfered with and cannot be taken away under any circumstances. Examples: freedom of thought, religion, and the prohibition of torture.
- Limited rights: can be restricted in certain circumstances. Example: your right to personal freedom can be restricted if you are detained after a criminal conviction.
- Qualified rights: an authority or government can sometimes interfere with them if it is in the interest of the wider community or to protect other people's rights. The interference must meet a social need, usually to protect the common good. Example: Covid-19 pandemic restrictions.

CLASS DISCUSSION: ARE OUR RIGHTS ALWAYS INALIENABLE?
- Human rights are not granted by governments or institutions. They are inherent to being human, so they cannot be revoked by anyone.
- Inalienable rights are rooted in human dignity: every human being has worth and should be treated with respect.
- Some argue inalienable rights may be limited in times of national emergency or to protect public safety. Against this: such limits can lead to abuse of power and violation of human rights.

KEY THINKER: MARTHA NUSSBAUM
- Governments and international organisations often use the word 'rights' when talking about people's basic human claims.
- Nussbaum believes a rights-based approach to what humans need for a fulfilling life does not go far enough.
- She is critical of other ways of measuring quality of life and development and proposes her own: the capabilities approach.
- Capabilities approach: an approach to human wellbeing that focuses on the actual capability of a person - what they can do based on what they have and what opportunities are open to them. It looks past what a person possesses to what they can achieve with it.
- She argues the approach considers the many parts of a person's quality of life and is needed in a modern era of vast inequalities.
- She believes liberalism must be challenged first, as she sees liberalism as a barrier to basic human rights.
- She argues that the economic policies of neoliberalism (a government approach that favours cutting government spending) lead to a denial of basic human rights.
- Governments should be more open to making the world better for the least well off and should care about welfare and basic rights. This is her idea of the 'social minimum'.
- Social minimum: an equal foundation or starting point for all people. It is based on the capabilities approach (freedom to achieve wellbeing is about what people can be and do). She argues it can accommodate all citizens, including vulnerable groups.

NUSSBAUM'S 10 CENTRAL CAPABILITIES (must be given to all citizens if rights are to be attained)
- 1 Life: being able to live a full, healthy life.
- 2 Health: being able to enjoy health, shelter and nourishment.
- 3 Bodily integrity: moving freely without assault, and choosing one's own partner.
- 4 Senses, imagination, thought: fully formed senses - arts, sciences, education; personal choice in music, literature, religion; full freedom of religious expression and expression.
- 5 Emotions: being able to fully engage in human emotions.
- 6 Practical reasoning: being able to make full, measured and logical decisions.
- 7 Affiliation: being able to affiliate with whoever you want, from friends to a political party.
- 8 Other species: living with concern for other species.
- 9 Play: being able to enjoy laughter, play and fun.
- 10 Control over one's environment: personal agency over marriage and politics.

NUSSBAUM ON EDUCATION
- She hopes education can 'cultivate humanity' and develop 'world citizens'.
- Education should be progressive, build critical thinking and foster independent minds.
- Strong link to Key Thinker Paulo Freire: a liberal education is needed so young people can reason and explain their own ideas rather than just absorbing others' ideas and not questioning authority.
- Quote: 'The failure to think critically produces a democracy in which people talk to each other but never have a genuine dialogue.'
- A thoughtful democracy needs citizens who can reason about their beliefs. It is bad for democracy if people vote based only on what the media and authorities tell them.

POSITIVE AND NEGATIVE RIGHTS
- Positive right: requires others to provide you with a service or good; you can demand that someone or some body does something for you. Example: the right to education, as the government must provide it. Economic, social and cultural rights are often linked with positive rights.
- Negative right: requires others to refrain from interfering in your actions; no action is needed. Example: the right to life - you only need to be left alone.
- Positive and negative rights often conflict. Example: the positive right to social welfare requires the Irish government to provide a service, which raises state spending and may mean higher taxes. This infringes a person's negative right not to have their money taken.
- Robert Nozick's view (speech bubble): positive rights interfere with others' freedom; you are forced to provide something for another, which is unfair.
- John Rawls's view (speech bubble): to give everyone equal rights and a base of equality we must provide for those who cannot provide for themselves; if positive rights mean taxing people for social welfare, he is in favour.

11.2 THE RIGHTS OF YOUNG PEOPLE
- Education is a fundamental human right and a tool for personal development, social inclusion and economic progress. The Irish Constitution recognises it as a fundamental right. (Links to Chapter 14.)
- Rights holder: a person or organisation that owns the legal rights to something. Everyone is a rights holder. The UDHR places the responsibility for providing rights on the state.
- Duty bearer: those responsible for promoting, protecting and fulfilling our human rights.
- In education, children are rights holders; the state and parents are duty bearers. The chapter summary also names teachers as duty bearers.
- Children's Rights Alliance (CRA): founded in 1995; unites over 140 members working to make Ireland one of the best places in the world to be a child; makes sure children's rights are respected in laws, policies and services. It says all children in Ireland have the right to education.
- Education Act 1998: requires the government to guarantee everyone living in Ireland 'a minimum level and quality of education appropriate to meeting the needs and abilities of that person'. Generally covers primary and second-level education.

ARTICLE 42 OF BUNREACHT NA hEIREANN (THE CONSTITUTION)
- 42.1: The State recognises the Family as the primary and natural educator of the child, and respects the inalienable right and duty of parents to provide for their children's religious, moral, intellectual, physical and social education, according to their means.
- 42.2: Parents are free to educate at home, in private schools, or in schools recognised or established by the State.
- 42.3.1: The State cannot force parents, against their conscience and lawful preference, to send children to State schools or any particular type of school.
- 42.3.2: But the State, as guardian of the common good, shall require that children receive a certain minimum education - moral, intellectual and social.
- 42.4: The State shall provide for free primary education, and try to give reasonable aid to private and corporate educational initiative, and provide other educational facilities when the public good requires, with regard for parents' rights, especially in religious and moral formation.
- Questions raised: children from poor backgrounds may not get the same education from their family (link to social mobility and social/cultural capital, Chapter 8); should home-schooling be allowed, and could a home-schooled child lose out on a full education?

THE UNCRC AND THE RIGHT TO EDUCATION
- The UN General Assembly adopted the UNCRC in 1989.
- It sets out how children should be treated and the rights of everyone under 18: survival, protection, development and participation rights.
- It sets a minimum standard that governments must meet in education, legal and social services, and healthcare.
- Ireland signed the Convention on 28 September 1992.
- The UNCRC defines a child as a 'human being below the age of 18 years' and sees children as rights holders entitled to special care, assistance and protection.
- Youth-friendly examples of UNCRC articles: Art 12 right to give your opinion and be listened to; Art 19 protection from being hurt and mistreated; Art 23 special education and care if you have a disability; Art 27 food, clothing, a safe place to live; Art 28 a good quality education; Art 29 education should develop your talents; Art 31 play and rest; Art 34 freedom from sexual abuse; Art 36 protection from any kind of exploitation; Art 42 right to know your rights; Articles 43 to 54 explain how governments and bodies like UNICEF will work to protect children.

CRA REPORT CARD 2023 - KEY FACTS AND STATISTICS
- 1,387 young people aged 18 to 24 homeless (December 2022).
- 95% of 8 to 12-year-olds own their own smart device.
- Children homeless in Ireland (December figures): 2,327 in 2020; 2,451 in 2021; 3,442 in 2022.
- 3,580 children and young people in Direct Provision (November 2022).
- 4,100 children waiting on a CAMHS appointment (September 2022).
- Over half a million primary school students to benefit from free school books.
- 228,007 children benefited from the School Meals Programme 2021/22.

ARTICLE 28 OF THE UNCRC (RIGHT TO EDUCATION) - achieved progressively and on the basis of equal opportunity. States shall:
- (a) Make primary education compulsory and free to all.
- (b) Encourage different forms of secondary education (general and vocational), make them available to every child, with measures like free education and financial help in need.
- (c) Make higher education accessible to all on the basis of capacity.
- (d) Make educational and vocational information and guidance available to all children.
- (e) Encourage regular school attendance and reduce drop-out rates.
- School discipline must respect the child's human dignity.
- Promote international cooperation in education, to end ignorance and illiteracy, with special attention to developing countries.

ARTICLE 29 OF THE UNCRC (AIMS OF EDUCATION) - education should develop:
- (a) The child's personality, talents and mental and physical abilities to their fullest potential.
- (b) Respect for human rights, fundamental freedoms and the UN Charter.
- (c) Respect for parents, the child's own cultural identity, language and values, the national values of the country, and other civilisations.
- (d) Preparation for responsible life in a free society - understanding, peace, tolerance, equality of sexes, friendship among all peoples.
- (e) Respect for the natural environment.
- People and bodies remain free to set up schools, as long as they meet the State's minimum standards.

ARTICLE 26 OF THE UDHR
- Everyone has the right to education. It shall be free at least in the elementary and fundamental stages. Elementary education shall be compulsory.
- Technical and professional education generally available; higher education equally accessible to all on the basis of merit.
- Education should develop the human personality, strengthen respect for human rights, promote understanding, tolerance and friendship among nations, racial and religious groups, and support UN peace work.
- Parents have a prior right to choose the kind of education their children get.

LINK BETWEEN THE UNCRC AND THE UDHR
- Both recognise education as a fundamental right for children.
- The UDHR was the first international legal instrument to recognise education as a right.
- The UNCRC (1989) builds on this for children and promotes social progress and the full development of the human personality.
- Both acknowledge education's role in social progress, better standards of life and full development of the personality.

IMPLEMENTING RIGHTS: 'MAXIMUM EXTENT OF THEIR AVAILABLE RESOURCES'
- By signing in 1992, Ireland committed under international law to respect, protect and fulfil children's rights.
- States must implement rights 'to the maximum extent of their available resources' - they must do all in their power to make sure rights are realised.
- Immediate obligation: states must take concrete, targeted steps, using all available resources, towards full achievement of rights. Ireland must ensure rights for all without discrimination and ensure a minimum level of rights for all citizens.
- Progressive realisation: full rights may be hard to achieve due to limits on knowledge and resources. The International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) accepts economic and social rights can only be achieved over time. Governments must keep making progress (legislative, financial and social steps).

THE UN COMMITTEE ON THE RIGHTS OF THE CHILD AND IRELAND
- An international group of experts that supervises how states implement the UNCRC.
- First examined Ireland in 1998. Ireland appeared for a third time in January 2016. Ireland made its most recent report in February 2022.
- 2022 Concluding Observations on education: welcomes the Free Education Scheme and increased funding in Budget 2023.
- Concerns: persistent barriers for disadvantaged children to quality education; lack of data broken down by ethnic origin, socioeconomic background and residence status; the setting up of special classes for children with disabilities.
- Recommendations: equal access for disadvantaged groups (Roma and Traveller children, asylum-seeking, refugee and migrant children, children with disabilities, socioeconomically disadvantaged children); change admissions law to ban priority for children or grandchildren of past pupils in oversubscribed schools; financial support for hidden costs of education; collect broken-down data on attendance, completion, outcomes, reduced timetables and after-school activities; inclusive education in mainstream schools for children with disabilities with adapted curricula and specialised teachers.

OTHER BODIES (GROUP WORK ROLES)
- Irish Government, Irish Citizens' Assembly (should represent Ireland's diverse population), UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, Children's Rights Alliance (grades the government in an annual report), and Comhairle na nOg (child and youth councils in local authorities for under-18s who cannot vote).

11.3 HOW IS IRELAND DOING? CHILD SAFETY ONLINE (UNCRC ARTICLES 19, 34 AND 36)
- In 2023 the CRA report card examined protection from abuse and neglect (Art 19) and from sexual and other exploitation (Arts 34 to 36), under Child Safety Online.
- The online world brings opportunities and risks, such as harmful content and cyberbullying.
- National survey: 62% of children aged 9 to 17 use social media; 25% saw or experienced something online that bothered them in the past year.
- The Irish public strongly supports government action, including rules for big tech companies and holding social media companies responsible for content.
- Law and policy had not kept pace with the online world.
- The EU Digital Services Act (DSA) recommends that platforms used by children adopt proportionate measures to protect minors, including standards and codes of conduct.
- Before 2023 the CRA graded Ireland 'C-' on Child Safety Online. Recommendations: tackle digital inclusion, protect children's safety online, improve digital literacy; the UN Committee recommended effective mechanisms for children's digital rights violations and reviewing laws to protect children from digital exploitation.
- In 2023 Ireland was graded 'A'. Why: the Online Safety and Media Regulation (OSMR) Act, which includes an Online Safety Commissioner and an individual complaints mechanism; asks platforms used by children to protect minors; sets up a new Media Commission to develop binding online safety codes and enforce them with audits and financial sanctions; the Commission also has a role in online safety education, research and media literacy.
- This shows the government as duty bearer facing the challenge of changing media, and the role of supranational and human rights bodies.

CHAPTER SUMMARY
- Human rights are rights we have simply because we are human.
- Universal = apply to all; inalienable = cannot be taken away; indivisible = interconnected.
- Absolute = cannot be restricted; limited = can be restricted in certain conditions; qualified = can be restricted for public interest or others' rights.
- Positive rights need action; negative rights need others not to interfere.
- Nussbaum: capabilities approach, social minimum, liberal education for critical, active citizens.
- Article 42 of the Constitution; Articles 28 and 29 UNCRC; Article 26 UDHR deal with education.
- Government, teachers and parents are duty bearers in education.
- Immediate obligation and progressive realisation; the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child examines Ireland's progress.

KEY TERMS
- Capabilities approach, social minimum, absolute rights, limited rights, qualified rights, positive rights, negative rights, rights holders, duty bearers, immediate obligation, progressive realisation.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words what it means for human rights to be universal, inalienable and indivisible.
rows.model_answer: Universal means every person everywhere is entitled to human rights, as Article 1 of the UDHR says all are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Inalienable means rights should not be taken away except in specific situations, such as limits on movement during Covid-19. Indivisible means rights depend on each other, so denying one right blocks enjoyment of others.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between an absolute right and a qualified right, giving an example of each.
rows.model_answer: An absolute right can never lawfully be interfered with or taken away, for example the prohibition of torture. A qualified right can be interfered with by the government if it meets a social need, such as protecting the common good or other people's rights. An example is the Covid-19 pandemic restrictions.

rows.prompt: Explain how positive and negative rights can conflict, using an example from the chapter.
rows.model_answer: A positive right needs someone to provide a service, such as social welfare from the government. Providing this raises state spending and may mean higher taxes. This can infringe a person's negative right not to have their money taken from them.

rows.prompt: Briefly explain Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach and her idea of the social minimum.
rows.model_answer: The capabilities approach looks past what a person possesses to what they can actually do and be with what they have and the opportunities open to them. Nussbaum says rights alone do not go far enough. The social minimum is an equal starting point for everyone, built on central capabilities such as life, health and play, which can include vulnerable groups.

rows.prompt: Explain the terms 'rights holder' and 'duty bearer' with reference to education.
rows.model_answer: A rights holder is a person or organisation that owns rights; everyone is a rights holder. A duty bearer is responsible for promoting, protecting and fulfilling those rights. In education, children are the rights holders, and the state and parents (and teachers) are the duty bearers.

rows.prompt: Name two things Article 42 of the Irish Constitution says about education.
rows.model_answer: Article 42 says the Family is the primary and natural educator of the child and parents are free to educate at home, in private schools or in State schools. It also says the State must require a certain minimum education and must provide for free primary education.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by 'immediate obligation' and 'progressive realisation'.
rows.model_answer: Immediate obligation means states must take concrete, targeted steps right away, using all available resources, including ensuring rights without discrimination and a minimum level of rights for all. Progressive realisation accepts that full rights, especially economic and social rights under the ICESCR, can only be achieved over time, but governments must keep making progress through legal, financial and social measures.

rows.prompt: Name two features of the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act that helped Ireland's grade improve.
rows.model_answer: The Act created an Online Safety Commissioner and an individual complaints mechanism. It also set up a new Media Commission to develop binding online safety codes and enforce them through audits and financial sanctions.

rows.prompt: Explain what it means for states to agree to act to implement rights 'to the maximum extent of their available resources'. Describe an Irish example. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: It means a state must do all in its power, using all the resources it has, to make sure rights are realised. This involves an immediate obligation to take concrete, targeted steps and provide a minimum level of rights without discrimination, and progressive realisation, where rights such as economic and social rights are achieved over time with continual progress. An Irish example is education: the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (2022) welcomed the Free Education Scheme and increased funding in Budget 2023, but recommended Ireland provide financial support to cover hidden costs of education and better access for Traveller, Roma and migrant children.
rows.marking_scheme: Explanation of the phrase: 4 marks (2 marks basic statement, 2 marks development, e.g. reference to immediate obligation or progressive realisation). Irish example: 6 marks (2 marks for naming a relevant example, 4 marks for development using evidence such as Budget 2023, Free Education Scheme or UN Committee recommendations).

rows.prompt: Study the source: 'Children homeless in Ireland (December figures): 2020 - 2,327; 2021 - 2,451; 2022 - 3,442. 3,580 children and young people in Direct Provision (November 2022). 4,100 children waiting on a CAMHS appointment (September 2022).' (CRA Report Card 2023). (a) What does the data show about child homelessness in Ireland? (b) Link one of these statistics to a right in the UNCRC. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: (a) The data shows child homelessness rose every year, from 2,327 in 2020 to 2,451 in 2021 and then sharply to 3,442 in 2022, an increase of over 1,100 children in two years. (b) The homelessness figure links to Article 27 of the UNCRC, the right to food, clothing, a safe place to live and basic needs being met. The CAMHS waiting list of 4,100 links to Article 24, the right to the best health care possible. These figures suggest the state as duty bearer is failing to fully meet its obligations to children.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 4 marks: correct trend identified (2 marks) with figures quoted (2 marks). (b) 6 marks: correct UNCRC right named (2 marks), clear link explained to the statistic (2 marks), comment on state as duty bearer or obligations (2 marks).

rows.prompt: Briefly explain Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach and outline her views on education. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: Nussbaum argues that a rights-based approach does not go far enough. Her capabilities approach looks at what a person can actually do and be with what they have and the opportunities available. She proposes a social minimum, an equal starting point for all, made up of ten central capabilities such as life, health, bodily integrity, affiliation and play, which can include vulnerable groups. She criticises neoliberal spending cuts as denying basic rights. On education, she wants it to 'cultivate humanity' and create 'world citizens', building critical thinking and independent minds, like Freire. She warns that 'the failure to think critically produces a democracy in which people talk to each other but never have a genuine dialogue.'
rows.marking_scheme: Capabilities approach explained: 4 marks (2 x 2 marks, e.g. focus on what people can do; social minimum; named capabilities). Views on education: 4 marks (2 x 2 marks, e.g. cultivate humanity/world citizens; critical thinking; link to Freire; democracy). Use of quote or developed example: 2 marks.

rows.prompt: 'Agreements such as the UNCRC are key in upholding the rights of young people in Ireland.' Discuss, referring to at least two thinkers and contemporary evidence. (80 marks)
rows.model_answer: Introduction: I agree that agreements like the UNCRC are key, as they set a minimum standard that the Irish state, as duty bearer, must meet for children as rights holders. Ireland signed the UNCRC on 28 September 1992 and committed under international law to respect, protect and fulfil children's rights to the maximum extent of its available resources. Paragraph 1 (education): Article 28 requires free, compulsory primary education and accessible secondary education; Article 29 says education should develop each child's talents fully. This builds on Article 26 of the UDHR, the first international instrument to recognise education as a right. In Ireland, Article 42 of the Constitution guarantees free primary education and the Education Act 1998 requires a minimum level and quality of education. Paragraph 2 (monitoring): The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child examines Ireland (first in 1998, again in 2016 and 2022). In 2022 it welcomed the Free Education Scheme and Budget 2023 funding but was concerned about barriers for disadvantaged children and special classes for children with disabilities. It recommended banning priority admission for children of past pupils and funding hidden costs. This pressure shows the agreement holds Ireland accountable. Paragraph 3 (real change): Child Safety Online moved from C- to A in the CRA Report Card 2023 after the OSMR Act created an Online Safety Commissioner and a Media Commission, protecting rights under Articles 19, 34 and 36. Paragraph 4 (counter-argument): The agreement alone is not enough. Child homelessness rose from 2,327 in 2020 to 3,442 in 2022, 3,580 children were in Direct Provision and 4,100 waited for CAMHS. Under progressive realisation, rights are achieved only over time, and Nozick would argue positive rights unfairly force taxpayers to provide for others. Paragraph 5 (thinkers): Nussbaum argues rights do not go far enough; we must look at children's real capabilities and guarantee a social minimum, and she criticises neoliberal cuts. Rawls supports taxing people to give everyone a base of equality. Conclusion: The UNCRC is key because it sets standards, enables monitoring and drives laws, but it must be backed by government spending and political will to be fully realised.
rows.marking_scheme: SEC-style discursive marking: Clear position on the statement stated and sustained (up to 10 marks). Knowledge and understanding of the UNCRC, related articles, key terms (rights holder, duty bearer, progressive realisation) (up to 20 marks). Use of at least two thinkers, one on the course, e.g. Nussbaum, Rawls, Nozick, applied to the argument (up to 15 marks). Contemporary evidence and data from Ireland, e.g. UN Committee 2022 observations, CRA Report Card 2023, OSMR Act, homelessness figures (up to 20 marks). Counter-arguments considered and evaluated (up to 10 marks). Structure, coherence and conclusion (up to 5 marks).
